Manila, P.I.
Friday, August 25
33
Dearest Debs-
We, Mr. Grooch, Mr. Ehmer and I, left Manila yesterday
morning at eight a.m. and arrived in
Iloilo (pronounced
E IO E LO) at eleven a.m. There, we were met by members of
the Lopez family who own about everything in and around
Ilo1lo;-boat lines, sugar centrals, warehouses, bus lines,
restaurants, eto.,
and among
the others, the Iloilo-Negros
Air Express Co., which owns two tri-motor Stinsons.
ships are operated between Iloilo, on the island of Iloilo,
and three small towns on the Island of Negros, on short runs
of not over twenty-five miles, making the distance in from
fifteen to seventeen minutes as against two hours by boat.
They also have a service to Manila, two hundred ninety miles
north, making two round trips per week.
We had an interesting trip down, but nothing of parti-
cular note.
We flew from Manila over Laguna de Bay, a large
lake south of Manila, and then a short distance over land,
up a valley between mountains five to six thousand feet high.
The country, even in the valleys, is intensively cultivated
only in small sections;-a few rice fields, a few truck farms
and orchards; many coconut tree groves and banana trees.
Leaving the island of Luzon, we flew a compass course
which carried us between the islands of Mindoro and Marindu-
que over, and always near some interesting little island,
deep green foliage standing out against light blue water,
island framed by a white sand beach.
Some islands had little,
whitewashed houses with red roofs on the edge of a clearing,
overlooking the sea.
We flew on across the island of ranay to Iloilo. The
Lopez boys had all the local celebrities out to greet
Governor of the Province, Mayor of Iloilo, etc. Then they
took Grooch and I, leaving thmer with the
plane, and went to
a camp which they
own on an island.
There we had a lunch,
combining the culinary arts of Philippine cooks with those of
the old Spanish regime. There were about seventy-five people
in the party, all men, and they certainly pulled right up to
the table and went to work like harvest hands on
• a Kansas
By the time Grooch and I had had a chance to look
around the place with Mr. Eugenio Lopez and pass
a few bon
mots his way, the beer was all gone, and most of the food.

Later on, they trotted out more food, but we had to get along
on coconut milk instead of beer. They had roast chicken,
cooked on a stick, the latter thrust thru the chicken from
end to end.
one end of the stick is placed firmly against
a rock and the other end is held by the operator or cook, who
turns said chicken around slowly over the hot coals.
very good.
We also had roast pig, which was delicious.
And the best ham
I have ever eaten,
tho I only had a small piece.
That was the
first line of defence which the Lopez boys had placed against
the onslaught of the guest shocktroops, and the ham
was taken
in the very first rush.
we also had corn on the cob, roasted,
which was fairly good, but like the depression, very
tough.
We got back to town about three o'clock, and went to
Fernando Lopez's house, and later into a business talk with the
two Lopez boys and their brother-in-law, Dr. Santos, and their
operations manager, one Lee Smith, who also serves as pilot.
After our business
conference, about six-thirty, we went to the
Smith's house for cocktails.
Lee Smith has been out here since
January; his wife, or rather first fiancé and now wife, came
all the way from Atlanta, Georgia, to marry him about two months
We then went to a party at the Lido restaurant, also owned
by the Lopez group. They had a fairly good orchestra, and we
had an exceptionally fine dinner with champagne, if you please.
The party broke up early.
Grooch and I stayed at the home of Mr. and Mrs. Fernando
Lopez.
We each had a room. The beds do not have box or any
kind of springs, and no mattress--just a sort of cane,
like the seat of a cane chair.
I have slept more comfortably.
I had a mosquito netting around my bed (the houses have no
screens) and while the mosquitos could not get at me, I could
hear them cruising around.
Their hum was occasionally drowned
out by the squeek of one of the many small lizards which are a
part of every well run Philippine household. The lizards are
little fellows, only about six inches long.
They live on flies
and mosquitos, and as far as 1 can see, there's no reason for
any poor little lizard to starve.
This morning, we rose at five a.m., which was no hardship
for me, in fact, 1 was glad to get up,
and had breakfast on
board one of the Lopez boats.
Then we took off for Zamboanga,
about two hundred sixty-five miles south of Monits, flying
almost due south from 1loilo.
we got to Zamboanga at about
nine thirty and landed just for a few minutes.
we had an
excellent chance to look over the harbor facilities which we
were told, and now know are not satisfactory for sea plane
landings.
we found a place, however, which should be 0.K.
in any kind of weather, altho ten miles from the town. The
